sentences.text: Palatodonta possessed a tall skull with a short, blunt snout. The premaxillae bore four large, chisel-shaped teeth that leaned forward. A single row of large teeth ran along the palatine bone parallel to the upper jaw. The lower jaw contained at least 14 sharp, narrow teeth that became larger and more robust toward the rear.
The animal had a very large, circular eye socket. The postorbital bridge was positioned low on the skull, exposing both temporal openings from the side.
Unlike the thick, blunt palatal teeth of placodonts, Palatodonta possessed thin, pointed palatal teeth resembling those of other reptiles.

The genus Palatodonta was first described by James M. Neenan, Nicole Klein, and Torsten M. Scheyer in 2013. The type species was discovered by amateur paleontologist Remco Bleeker in the summer of 2010 at the Silbeco quarry near Winterswijk. The only known fossil is a well-preserved skull of a juvenile individual designated as holotype TW480000470.
Researchers once interpreted Palatodonta as a transitional form between placodonts and less specialized reptiles.

In 2013, Palatodonta was classified as a basal placodontiform related to the marine reptile group known as placodonts. A 2023 study reclassified Palatodonta as a sauropterygomorph and the sister taxon to Eusaurosphargis.
Palatodonta lived during the early Middle Triassic, specifically the early Anisian stage, in the Netherlands.
It is debated whether Palatodonta belongs within Sauropterygia; a 2023 study places it as a sauropterygomorph sister to Eusaurosphargis, close to but outside the group.
